meta.title: Swahili A2 Elementary
meta.subtitle: 750 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Swahili → English (see the Swahili, recall the meaning) and English → Swahili (see an English meaning, recall the Swahili). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 750 words for an elementary learner, aligned to A2 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand sentences and frequently used expressions related to areas of most immediate relevance' — a learner here is able to communicate in simple and routine tasks requiring a simple and direct exchange of information on familiar and routine matters, and to describe in simple terms aspects of their background, immediate environment and matters in areas of immediate need. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Swahili that could be used here, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 269 of the 750 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — the months and seasons, the land, the weather and animals, clothes, the home and the kitchen, food and cooking, work and jobs, school, travel and transport, the town, health, feelings, free time, the everyday verbs of these, describing things and people, time words, and the words that join one clause to the next — and the other 481 are the commonest remaining words, counted by the WHOLE word (every form of a noun, every conjugated form of a verb added together) in two collections of real Swahili, film and television subtitles and the Global Voices news site, a word having to be common in both. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first. Verbs are shown as their infinitive (kusoma, to read) with their stem (-soma), which every tense is built on, and their negative infinitive; adjectives and possessives as their stem (-zuri, -angu) with the forms they take after three of the noun classes. The 464 nouns show their class, which every adjective, verb and possessive agrees with, and their plural; there are 201 verbs. Real example sentences come with 633 of the 750 words, three apiece for 436 of them, with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, noun classes and forms: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: counted from OpenSubtitles 2024 and Global Voices (CC BY 3.0), both as distributed by OPUS. Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
